resources.string: Middle ear: oblique cutaway from eardrum to oval window
Ossicular chain
Eardrum
The tympanic membrane separates the ear canal from the air-filled middle ear. The malleus handle attaches to it at the umbo, the deepest point of the membrane.
Malleus
The head of the malleus meets the incus above the eardrum. Its handle extends down along the inner side of the eardrum to the umbo.
Incus
The body of the incus meets the malleus high in the middle ear. Its long process descends to a small joint with the head of the stapes.
Stapes
Two slender branches give the stapes its stirrup shape. They join the head, which touches the incus, to the footplate seated in the oval window.
Oval window
The oval window opens into the inner-ear vestibule. A flexible ring seals the stapes footplate to its rim while allowing the footplate to move.
Round window
A flexible membrane covers this opening below the oval window, at the basal end of the scala tympani. It can move as the stapes displaces inner-ear fluid.
Cochlea: simplified cross-section through one turn
Cochlear cross-section
Scala vestibuli
This perilymph-filled chamber lies above the cochlear duct, separated from it by Reissner’s membrane. Toward the base it opens into the vestibule.
Reissner’s membrane
This thin, sloping membrane forms the roof of the cochlear duct. It separates the duct’s endolymph from the perilymph of the scala vestibuli.
Cochlear duct
Also called the scala media, this wedge-shaped chamber contains endolymph. Its roof slopes toward the outer wall, and the organ of Corti sits on its floor.
Organ of Corti
The hearing sensory epithelium sits inside the cochlear duct on the basilar membrane. Its hair cells lie beneath the tectorial membrane.
Basilar membrane
This membrane spans from the inner bony shelf to the outer wall. It supports the organ of Corti and separates the cochlear duct from the scala tympani below.
Scala tympani
This perilymph-filled chamber lies below the cochlear partition. At the base it ends at the round window; at the tip of the coil it joins the scala vestibuli.
Vestibular labyrinth: semicircular canals and otolith organs
Canals and otolith organs
Anterior canal
This upward arch houses the anterior semicircular duct, one of the two steeply oriented ducts that sense head rotation. Its non-ampullary end joins the posterior duct in a shared branch.
Posterior canal
The posterior semicircular duct runs in a different steep plane from the anterior duct. One end widens into an ampulla and the other joins the shared branch.
Lateral canal
The lateral canal houses the more nearly horizontal semicircular duct. Both ends open into the utricle separately from the shared branch of the other two ducts.
Posterior ampulla
This swelling of the posterior duct contains a sensory ridge capped by a gelatinous cupula. During head rotation, relative endolymph motion deflects the cupula.
Utricle
The flattened upper sac receives the semicircular ducts. Crystals called otoconia overlie its mostly horizontal sensory patch, which responds to linear acceleration and tilt relative to gravity.
Saccule
The smaller sac sits below the utricle. Its sensory patch is more nearly vertical and also carries otoconia; it is especially sensitive to vertical linear acceleration.
